_comment: R&D decisions (ui-spec.md component 26, user's idea 2026-10-10). Ids are kept in saved state and turn reports: never rename or reuse one. Sizes are relative: RELIABILITY in seasons of the component's R&D gain, FUNDS and an option's cost as a share of a season's funding. Text fits both agencies; {name} and {second} are the people an option took. The pools were grown on 2026-10-25 to about twenty per type (fewer for pairing and hands-on), each fitting rockets, payloads or both.

decisions.headline: Pay for a static test firing?
decisions.text: The engine team wants to bolt the stage to the test stand and fire it, held down, before anything else is built around it. A clean run would settle a lot of arguments.

options.label: Pay for the full firing
options.shows: 70 % chance of about two seasons' gain, else about half a season's.

outcomes.headline: The firing went clean
outcomes.text: The stage ran its full time without a flicker in the gauges. The engineers want to push it harder next time.

outcomes.headline: A rough run
outcomes.text: The engine shut down early on a sensor fault. The data is thin, but something was learned.

options.label: Fire it at half power
options.shows: Sure to give about half a season's gain.

outcomes.headline: A careful half-power run
outcomes.text: Nothing dramatic, nothing broken, and a little more known about the engine.

outcomes.headline: No firing this time
outcomes.text: The stage goes back to the assembly hall untested.

decisions.recall: Last time the held-down firing went clean.
decisions.headline: Fire it at full thrust
decisions.text: Encouraged by the clean firing, the engine team wants to run the stage at full thrust for its whole burn time. If it holds, the design is proven; if it doesn't, the test stand may need rebuilding.

options.label: Run it at full thrust
options.shows: 60 % chance of about three seasons' gain; a failure costs about a season's.

outcomes.headline: Full thrust, full time
outcomes.text: The stage roared for its whole burn and shut down on command. The crew on the stand cheered.

outcomes.headline: A turbine let go
outcomes.text: A turbine blade failed at full speed and took the pump with it. The engineers will spend weeks on what is left.

outcomes.headline: Not yet
outcomes.text: The full-thrust run is put off.

decisions.recall: The full-thrust firing held all the way.
decisions.headline: One last endurance run
decisions.text: The engine has passed every firing so far. One long run, twice the burn time, would show where it wears out first.

options.label: Run it twice as long
options.shows: 50 % chance of about four seasons' gain; a failure costs about a season and a half's.

outcomes.headline: It just kept going
outcomes.text: The engine ran twice its burn time and came off the stand scorched but whole. The design is settled.

outcomes.headline: The chamber burned through
outcomes.text: Late in the run the chamber wall burned through. Now everyone knows where it wears out, and it cost an engine.

outcomes.headline: Enough testing
outcomes.text: The engine goes into production as it is.

decisions.headline: A week in the vacuum chamber?
decisions.text: The test lab has a free slot in its vacuum chamber. A week of airless cold and heat would show how the craft copes in space before it ever goes there.

options.label: Book the chamber
options.shows: 75 % chance of about two seasons' gain, else about half a season's.

outcomes.headline: A week in space, on the ground
outcomes.text: Every system worked through the cold nights and hot days. The lab offers a longer run.

outcomes.headline: The chamber leaked
outcomes.text: A seal in the chamber failed on the second day and the test was stopped. Half a week of data is better than none.

options.label: Let another team have the slot

outcomes.headline: The slot goes elsewhere
outcomes.text: Another team takes the chamber.

decisions.recall: Last time the craft came through a week in the vacuum chamber.
decisions.headline: A month in the chamber
decisions.text: The lab can keep the craft in vacuum for a month: as long as a real mission. It would find the slow faults a week can't.

options.label: Keep it in for a month
options.shows: 65 % chance of about three seasons' gain; a failure costs about a season's.

outcomes.headline: A month without a fault
outcomes.text: Thirty days of vacuum and the craft is still talking to the ground station.

outcomes.headline: A slow leak cooked the electronics
outcomes.text: In the third week a coolant leak ruined the electronics box. It will have to be rebuilt.

outcomes.headline: Enough of the chamber
outcomes.text: The craft goes back to the assembly room.

decisions.headline: Pay for a second round of inspections?
decisions.text: The quality office wants every weld and wire checked twice. It would slow nobody down, but the inspectors have to be paid.

options.label: Pay for the inspections
options.shows: Sure to give about a season's gain.

outcomes.headline: Faults found before they flew
outcomes.text: The inspectors find a cracked bracket and two loose connectors. Nobody likes being checked, but everyone is glad.

outcomes.headline: One round of checks
outcomes.text: The work goes on as it was.

decisions.headline: Rent time in the wind tunnel?
decisions.text: A university wind tunnel can take a scale model of the rocket. The aerodynamicists want to see how the air flows over the nose and the joints between the stages as it nears the speed of sound, where the slide rules stop being trustworthy.

options.label: Rent it for a week
options.shows: 80 % chance of about a season's gain, else nothing.

outcomes.headline: A week of smoke and shadows
outcomes.text: The shadow pictures show a shock wave sitting where nobody expected it. The fairing gets a gentler curve.

outcomes.headline: The model broke loose
outcomes.text: On the second day the model shook itself off its sting and wrecked a screen. The rest of the week went on repairs.

options.label: Rent it for a month
options.shows: 70 % chance of about two seasons' gain, else about half a season's.

outcomes.headline: Every speed, every angle
outcomes.text: A month of runs maps the whole climb through the air. The engineers know now where the loads peak, and by how much.

outcomes.headline: A month of queues
outcomes.text: A military project jumped the queue twice. Only a week's worth of runs got done.

outcomes.headline: No tunnel
outcomes.text: The model stays on a shelf in the drawing office.

decisions.headline: X-ray every weld?
decisions.text: The welds have all passed by eye. The materials lab offers to X-ray every one of them, which would show any bubble or crack hiding inside the metal. It is slow and costly, and it may find nothing.

options.label: X-ray them all
options.shows: 50 % chance of about two and a half seasons' gain, else nothing.

outcomes.headline: A hidden void
outcomes.text: One film shows a dark bubble inside a weld that looked perfect from outside. It would have opened under load. The welder's whole batch is redone.

outcomes.headline: Every weld clean
outcomes.text: Hundreds of films and not a flaw among them. The welders are insufferable for a week.

options.label: X-ray a sample of one in ten
options.shows: 20 % chance of about two seasons' gain, else nothing.

outcomes.headline: The sample caught one
outcomes.text: A crack turned up in the sample, and the lab traced it to a single bad spool of filler wire.

outcomes.headline: The sample was clean
outcomes.text: The films show nothing. Whether the other nine in ten are as good, nobody can say.

outcomes.headline: Passed by eye
outcomes.text: The welds go into the hardware as inspected.

decisions.headline: Build a unit just for testing?
decisions.text: Every test so far has been careful, because the only unit is the one that will fly. The workshop could build a second one that nobody minds damaging.

options.label: Build the test unit
options.shows: 75 % chance of about two seasons' gain, else about half a season's.

outcomes.headline: A unit to be rough with
outcomes.text: With a spare to spare, the testers stop tiptoeing, and the faults come out faster. Someone has already asked what it would take to break it.

outcomes.headline: Built late
outcomes.text: The second unit took the workshop twice as long as planned and arrived when the tests it was for were over.

outcomes.headline: One unit, handled gently
outcomes.text: The tests go on, carefully.

decisions.recall: Last time the workshop built a test unit nobody minds damaging.
decisions.headline: Load it until it breaks?
decisions.text: The stress engineers want to load the spare unit in the test rig, more and more, until something gives. Where it breaks tells them what their calculations got wrong. If it breaks early, the flight unit has the same weakness.

options.label: Load it to failure
options.shows: Sure to give at least a season's gain; more if it breaks early.

outcomes.headline: It broke too early, on the ground
outcomes.text: A mounting gave way well short of what the calculations promised. On the flight unit it would have failed in flight. Now it gets thicker.

outcomes.headline: It held far past the flight loads
outcomes.text: The rig ran out of strength before the unit did. The calculations were right, and now everyone knows it.

outcomes.headline: A spare on the shelf
outcomes.text: The test unit goes into storage, whole.

decisions.headline: Fire a batch of explosive bolts?
decisions.text: The stages come apart in flight on explosive bolts, and every bolt can only be tested once: by firing it. The engineers want to fire fifty from the same production lot to find out if the lot is any good.

options.label: Fire fifty of them
options.shows: Sure to give some gain: about half a season's if all fifty fire, two seasons' if a dud turns up.

outcomes.headline: Two duds in fifty
outcomes.text: Two bolts didn't fire. The whole lot is thrown out, and the supplier finds damp powder in one drum. A stage that wouldn't let go would have doomed a flight.

outcomes.headline: Fifty bangs, fifty clean
outcomes.text: Every bolt fired on command. The lot is cleared for flight.

outcomes.headline: On paper
outcomes.text: The lot goes into the hardware with its certificate.

decisions.headline: Hire a computer for the trajectories?
decisions.text: The ascent has been worked out by a room of people with desk calculators. A company with one of the new electronic computers offers to run thousands of trajectories, every wind and every engine fault, in a few nights.

options.label: Hire the computer
options.shows: 60 % chance of about two and a half seasons' gain, else nothing.

outcomes.headline: A thousand flights in a week
outcomes.text: The printouts show the rocket tumbling in a strong crosswind the hand calculations never tried. The steering gets more authority.

outcomes.headline: A wrong sign in the program
outcomes.text: Every trajectory flew backwards: one sign was wrong in the program, and nobody noticed until the money was spent.

options.label: Give the calculators more hands
options.shows: Sure to give about half a season's gain.

outcomes.headline: More pencils
outcomes.text: Four more people at the desk calculators work through a dozen extra cases. Slow, but every number is checked twice.

outcomes.headline: As calculated
outcomes.text: The ascent stays as the calculators worked it out.

decisions.headline: Hot, then cold, then hot again?
decisions.text: In orbit the craft will swing from sunlight to shadow and back every lap. The lab can do the same in a climate cabinet, heating and freezing it in turn, to find the solder joints that crack.

options.label: Run twenty cycles
options.shows: 70 % chance of about two seasons' gain, else about half a season's.

outcomes.headline: Twenty swings, two cracked joints
outcomes.text: Two joints cracked on the boards, and both are redone with more give in the wires. The lab says a real mission is hundreds of swings, not twenty.

outcomes.headline: The cabinet stuck at hot
outcomes.text: The cabinet's thermostat failed and cooked the boards for a day. Some data, and a lot of scorched wiring.

outcomes.headline: No cycling
outcomes.text: The boards go into the craft as they are.

decisions.recall: Last time twenty hot and cold cycles found two cracked joints.
decisions.headline: A hundred cycles
decisions.text: A real mission swings between sun and shadow hundreds of times. The lab offers a hundred cycles, running day and night for a month, to find the faults that take time to grow.

options.label: Run a hundred
options.shows: 60 % chance of about three seasons' gain; a failure costs about a season's.

outcomes.headline: A hundred swings, no harm
outcomes.text: After a month of heat and frost every board still passes its checks. The craft will not fail by slow cracking.

outcomes.headline: Worn out by the test
outcomes.text: By cycle eighty the main harness had fatigued at its clamps. The fix is known now, but the boards are scrap and must be built again.

outcomes.headline: Enough cycling
outcomes.text: The cabinet goes to another team.

decisions.headline: A night on the pad, fully loaded?
decisions.text: Nobody knows what a long hold does to the rocket. The pad crew could load it with propellant and leave it standing through a cold night, watching what frosts up and what leaks.

options.label: Hold it overnight
options.shows: 65 % chance of about two seasons' gain; else about half a season's lost.

outcomes.headline: A long, cold night
outcomes.text: By dawn a line of frost had shown where the insulation was thin, and one valve was sticking. Both are fixed before any real countdown.

outcomes.headline: Ice cracked a valve
outcomes.text: Ice built up in a vent valve overnight and cracked its body as it thawed. The valve is redesigned, and the test pad loses a week.

outcomes.headline: No long hold
outcomes.text: The rocket stays in its hangar.

decisions.headline: Bring in outside reviewers?
decisions.text: A board of retired engineers from aircraft and missile firms will read the drawings and test records for a fee. Fresh eyes find things, but they also find things that are not really there.

options.label: Hire the board
options.shows: 50 % chance of about two and a half seasons' gain, else about half a season's.

outcomes.headline: They found a real one
outcomes.text: An old missile engineer spots a mounting that worked loose on a missile he built years ago. Same design, same flaw. It is changed at once.

outcomes.headline: A long list of small things
outcomes.text: The board's report runs to forty pages. Most of it is matters of taste; a few points are worth fixing.

options.label: Our own people know it best

outcomes.headline: No outside review
outcomes.text: The drawings stay in the building.

decisions.headline: A ride on a sounding rocket?
decisions.text: A research institute is launching a small sounding rocket to the edge of space and has room for a few kilograms. The engineers could fly the craft's most doubtful instrument on it, for a few minutes of real space.

options.label: Buy the ride
options.shows: 55 % chance of about three seasons' gain, else nothing.

outcomes.headline: Five minutes in space
outcomes.text: The instrument worked, then misbehaved in a way no chamber ever showed. The telemetry tells the engineers exactly why.

outcomes.headline: The sounding rocket failed
outcomes.text: The little rocket veered off and was destroyed by the range officer. The instrument was never found.

outcomes.headline: No ride
outcomes.text: Someone else's experiment takes the space.

decisions.headline: Pressure the tanks past their limit?
decisions.text: The tank shop wants to fill a flight tank with water and pressurise it to half as much again as it will ever see in flight. A tank that holds is proven. A tank that splits is a tank that would have split anyway.

options.label: Run the proof test
options.shows: 75 % chance of about a season and a half's gain; else about a season's lost.

outcomes.headline: It held
outcomes.text: The tank swelled a hair's width and came back. Every seam is now known to be good.

outcomes.headline: A seam split
outcomes.text: At ninety per cent of the test pressure a seam opened with a crack like a rifle shot and flooded the bay. A new tank, a new seam design, and a lost season.

outcomes.headline: To flight pressure only
outcomes.text: The tank passes its usual check.

decisions.headline: Book the antenna range?
decisions.text: The craft's antennas have only been tested one at a time. On an outdoor antenna range the whole craft could be turned slowly on a tower while a receiver across the field listens, to find out where the signal fades.

options.label: Book the range
options.shows: 75 % chance of about a season and a half's gain, else nothing.

outcomes.headline: A blind spot found
outcomes.text: Turned on the tower, the craft goes silent at one angle: its own body blocks the antenna. A second antenna on the far side fixes it.

outcomes.headline: Rained off
outcomes.text: A week of storms, and a range that can't be used in rain. The booking ran out.

outcomes.headline: No range
outcomes.text: The antennas keep their bench results.

decisions.headline: Balance it on the spin table?
decisions.text: A craft that is even slightly lopsided wobbles when it spins or turns. The balancing lab can spin it up on a table and say exactly where to add a few grams of lead.

options.label: Spin it up
options.shows: 90 % chance of about a season's gain; else about half a season's lost.

outcomes.headline: True to the gram
outcomes.text: Three small weights in the right places, and the craft spins as smooth as a top.

outcomes.headline: A bracket let go at speed
outcomes.text: A loose bracket flew off at full speed and dented the table's guard. It was badly fastened: better found here, but the repairs take time.

outcomes.headline: Balanced on paper
outcomes.text: The weights stay where the drawings put them.

decisions.headline: Switch everything on at once?
decisions.text: Each of the craft's systems works on its own. Nobody has yet switched them all on together in a screened room, where the engineers could hear if one system's noise upsets another's.

options.label: Book the screened room
options.shows: 70 % chance of about a season and a half's gain, else about half a season's.

outcomes.headline: The recorder deafened the radio
outcomes.text: Every time the tape recorder's motor started, the receiver went deaf for a second. Shielding round the motor cures it.

outcomes.headline: All quiet
outcomes.text: Nothing interfered with anything. A short report, and a little more confidence.

options.label: They each work on their own

outcomes.headline: Not tested together
outcomes.text: The systems meet for the first time on the launch pad.

decisions.headline: Send it up on a balloon?
decisions.text: A high-altitude balloon can carry a test unit to thirty kilometres, above almost all the air, and keep it there for hours in the cold and the sunlight. It is the nearest thing to space that doesn't need a rocket.

options.label: Launch the balloon
options.shows: 65 % chance of about two seasons' gain, else nothing.

outcomes.headline: Six hours near the black sky
outcomes.text: The test unit floated for six hours and came down on its parachute in a farmer's field. Its readings show the electronics running cold. The balloon team offers a longer flight.

outcomes.headline: The balloon burst early
outcomes.text: The thin plastic split at ten kilometres in the jet stream, and the unit came down in a lake.

outcomes.headline: No balloon
outcomes.text: The balloon team flies someone else's instruments.

decisions.recall: Last time a balloon carried a test unit to the edge of space for six hours.
decisions.headline: Two days aloft
decisions.text: The balloon team has a bigger envelope that can float for two days, through a whole night at altitude. The test unit would meet its first real night: hours of cold with nothing but its batteries.

options.label: Fly for two days
options.shows: 55 % chance of about three seasons' gain; else about a season's lost.

outcomes.headline: Through the night and out
outcomes.text: The unit came through the night with its heaters cycling just as designed, and was recovered whole. The thermal design is settled.

outcomes.headline: Drifted out to sea
outcomes.text: The winds changed overnight and carried the balloon far out over the water. The unit and its records were lost, and a new one must be built.

outcomes.headline: No second flight
outcomes.text: The balloon goes back in its crate.

decisions.headline: Send a dummy load on the journey first?
decisions.text: The hardware will travel hundreds of kilometres by rail and road to the launch site. The transport office could first send a dummy of the same weight, packed with shock recorders, to see what the journey does to it.

options.label: Send the dummy
options.shows: Sure to give about half a season's gain; 40 % chance of about two seasons' instead.

outcomes.headline: A knock nobody expected
outcomes.text: The recorders show a jolt three times the packing limit, at a shunting yard. The crates get new springs and the railway gets a stern letter.

outcomes.headline: A gentle ride
outcomes.text: The journey was smoother than the packing was designed for. One less worry.

options.label: Pack it well and send it

outcomes.headline: Packed and trusted
outcomes.text: The crates are built to the usual standard.

decisions.headline: Analyse every load of propellant?
decisions.text: The propellant arrives by tanker with a certificate from the plant. The chemistry lab offers to test a sample from every load for water, rust and other dirt that clogs filters and injectors.

options.label: Test every load
options.shows: 30 % chance of about two and a half seasons' gain, else about half a season's.

outcomes.headline: A dirty tanker
outcomes.text: One load is full of rust flakes from an old tanker. It would have clogged the injector in seconds. The plant changes its tankers.

outcomes.headline: Clean, load after load
outcomes.text: Every sample passes. The lab does notice the filters could be finer, and they are changed.

outcomes.headline: Certified clean
outcomes.text: The tankers unload as usual.

decisions.headline: Build a full-size mockup?
decisions.text: On paper everything fits. The technicians who will have to assemble it want a full-size mockup to try their hands and tools on before the real parts arrive.

options.label: A wooden mockup
options.shows: Sure to give about half a season's gain.

outcomes.headline: Plywood and paint
outcomes.text: The mockup shows two connectors no wrench can reach. Small fixes, cheaply found.

options.label: A metal mockup with real wiring
options.shows: 70 % chance of about two seasons' gain, else about half a season's.

outcomes.headline: Every cable routed
outcomes.text: Routing real cables through real metal finds a harness that rubs on a sharp edge, and a dozen smaller snags.

outcomes.headline: The mockup lagged the design
outcomes.text: By the time the metal mockup was built, the drawings had moved on. Half of it no longer matched.

outcomes.headline: Straight to hardware
outcomes.text: The technicians will find out when the parts arrive.

decisions.headline: Balloon tanks on the pad
decisions.text: The night crew let the pressure drop in the rocket's thin-walled tanks while it stood empty on the pad. The chief engineer storms in and asks the room what would have happened.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: It would crumple under its own weight

outcomes.headline: Exactly right
outcomes.text: The tanks are held up by their own pressure, like a balloon. The chief engineer nods and puts a pressure alarm on every pad.

options.label: Nothing: the steel holds it up

outcomes.headline: Wrong, and costly
outcomes.text: The steel is thinner than paper in places. The engineers lose a week convincing the night crew to take the pressure seriously.

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: The tanks were empty. The real danger goes unaddressed, and a second scare follows the next week.

outcomes.headline: Better ask than guess
outcomes.text: The chief engineer explains it and moves on.

decisions.headline: Three valves in a row
decisions.text: A design review stops at a part with three valves that all have to work, each tested at 95 % reliable. The reviewer asks how reliable the three are together.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: The team signs off a part far weaker than it thinks. It shows up in testing a month later.

outcomes.headline: Right: the odds multiply
outcomes.text: Three parts that must all work are only as good as the product of their odds. The team redesigns it with two valves in parallel.

options.label: Over 99 %: three are safer than one

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: That's true of spares that back each other up, not of parts that must all work. The weak spot stays in the design.

outcomes.headline: Better ask than guess
outcomes.text: The reviewer works it through on the blackboard.

decisions.headline: Why so blunt?
decisions.text: A visiting official asks why the craft's heat shield is round and blunt instead of pointed like a bullet. The engineers look to you for the answer.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: Pointed would cut through the air and heat up less

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: A pointed shape keeps the hot shock wave right against the skin. The official leaves with the wrong idea and asks for a redesign study.

options.label: The blunt shape pushes a shock wave out ahead and keeps the heat off

outcomes.headline: Right
outcomes.text: Most of the heat stays in the air the shock wave pushes aside. The official is impressed, and so are the engineers.

outcomes.headline: Not the reason
outcomes.text: Room is a side effect. The engineers spend an afternoon setting the record straight.

outcomes.headline: The engineers explain
outcomes.text: The chief designer gives the official a short talk on shock waves.

decisions.headline: The hardest minute
decisions.text: The structures team is deciding where to add stiffening, and the chief asks the room: at what moment of the climb is the rocket squeezed and shaken hardest by the air?
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: At liftoff, where the air is thickest

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: At liftoff the rocket is barely moving, and slow air pushes gently. The stiffening goes to the wrong end of the rocket.

options.label: About a minute up, ten to fifteen kilometres high

outcomes.headline: Right: max Q
outcomes.text: By then it is fast, and the air is still thick enough to push hard. After that the thinning air wins. The stiffening goes where the push peaks.

options.label: At engine cutoff, when it's fastest

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: By cutoff the air is so thin it hardly pushes at all, however fast the rocket goes. A season goes on stiffening that wasn't needed.

outcomes.headline: Better ask than guess
outcomes.text: The chief draws the curve on the board: speed rising, air thinning, and the push peaking in between.

decisions.headline: Why always east?
decisions.text: A new range officer, fresh from the artillery, asks why every orbital launch heads east. Pointing the rocket another way would keep the falling stages clear of a village he is worried about.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: The high winds blow east and push it along

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: The winds are a nuisance, not a help. The range officer goes away thinking the direction doesn't matter much, and the argument costs weeks.

options.label: The Earth's spin gives it a free push that way

outcomes.headline: Right
outcomes.text: The pad is already moving east at hundreds of metres a second. Launch west and the rocket has to cancel that first. The range officer finds another way to keep the village safe.

options.label: The tracking stations are all to the east

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: The stations were put where the rockets go, not the other way round. The range officer asks for a new station to the north.

outcomes.headline: The flight planners explain
outcomes.text: A flight planner spins a globe on the desk and shows him.

decisions.headline: Before the restart
decisions.text: After a long coast in orbit, an engine has to light again. The test plan has a blank at the top, and the reviewer asks what must happen in the seconds before the engine starts.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: Warm the propellant so it lights

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: Warm or cold, propellant floating in blobs won't feed a pump. The plan goes out with the real problem unsolved.

options.label: Fire small rockets to settle the propellant

outcomes.headline: Right: settle it first
outcomes.text: A short push from small rockets and the floating propellant drifts back over the outlets, so the engine gets liquid, not gas. It goes at the top of the plan.

options.label: Spin the craft so the engine keeps pointing

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: Spinning flings the propellant to the tank walls, away from the outlet. The first restart test starves the engine.

outcomes.headline: Better ask than guess
outcomes.text: The reviewer fills in the blank and explains it.

decisions.headline: Where's the igniter?
decisions.text: A new technician has gone over the drawings of the small thrusters twice and can't find an igniter anywhere. Is it a mistake in the drawings? Everyone looks at you.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: No mistake: the two liquids burst into flame when they meet

outcomes.headline: Right: hypergolic
outcomes.text: Open two valves and the thruster runs, close them and it stops, with no spark to fail. The technician also learns why those liquids are handled in sealed suits.

outcomes.headline: Wrong, and expensive
outcomes.text: An igniter is designed for a thruster that never needed one, and the extra part adds a new way to fail. Someone senior catches it a season later.

options.label: The hot chamber relights it from the last burn

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: A thruster that waits an hour between puffs is stone cold. The technician spends a week looking for a heater that doesn't exist.

outcomes.headline: Better ask than guess
outcomes.text: The propulsion lead explains, and adds that the liquids eat through seals.

decisions.headline: No gravity up there?
decisions.text: A reporter visiting the assembly room writes that the craft will be beyond the pull of gravity, so nothing inside needs to be tied down. The press office asks you to check the story before it runs.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: It's right: gravity stops a little way up

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: The story runs, and a junior designer believes it too. A batch of loose fittings has to be found and fastened.

options.label: Gravity is almost as strong there; everything just falls together

outcomes.headline: Right: falling, not floating
outcomes.text: Without gravity the craft would fly off in a straight line. The story is fixed, and the designers fasten everything twice: a loose screw floats into the worst places.

options.label: The craft's spin cancels gravity out

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: The story runs with the wrong reason, and the engineers spend days answering letters about it.

outcomes.headline: The engineers check it
outcomes.text: The story waits a day while a physicist rewrites the paragraph.

decisions.headline: How long is a pass?
decisions.text: The operations team is writing the command plan and wants to know how long one ground station can talk to the craft each time it flies over, in an orbit about 200 km up.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: Most of the lap: radio goes round the curve of the Earth

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: Radio travels in straight lines, like light. The plan crams an hour of commands into a pass that ends after a few minutes.

outcomes.headline: Right
outcomes.text: The craft crosses one station's sky in minutes. The plan splits the commands across stations and stores the readings on board for the next pass.

options.label: Only while it's night at the station

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: Daylight doesn't stop radio. Half the passes go unused while the plan waits for dark.

outcomes.headline: Better ask than guess
outcomes.text: A tracking engineer draws the horizon on the board and works it out.

decisions.headline: A little lower?
decisions.text: To save the rocket some work, a planner wants to fly the craft at about 215 km instead of 360 km. “It's still in space,” the planner says. “What difference can 150 km make?”
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: None: there's no air at either height

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: There's a trace of air at both, and far more at the lower one. The plan goes ahead until an orbit specialist stops it, a season later.

options.label: The lower one falls in months, the higher one stays up for years

outcomes.headline: Right: height buys time
outcomes.text: Sputnik 1 dipped to about 215 km and fell in three months; Explorer 1, never below about 358 km, stayed up for twelve years. The planner keeps the higher orbit.

options.label: The lower one stays up longer: gravity holds it tighter

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: Gravity holds both. It's the air that drags a low orbit down, and the lower plan is adopted for a while.

outcomes.headline: Better ask than guess
outcomes.text: An orbit specialist explains, and the decision is put off.

decisions.headline: The counter went quiet
decisions.text: On a test flight the radiation counter read normally low down, then dropped to zero on the high part of every orbit. The instrument team wants to replace the counter. A physicist asks you what zero means.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: Space is empty of radiation up there

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: The electronics are left unshielded for that part of the orbit, and the next unit fails in the radiation test.

options.label: The counter breaks in the cold

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: A new counter is built and fails in exactly the same way. A season is spent on a part that was working.

options.label: It was swamped by so much radiation it stopped counting

outcomes.headline: Right: too much, not too little
outcomes.text: Like a microphone overloaded by a roar. It is just what happened to Explorer 1 in 1958. The electronics get shielding and sturdier parts.

outcomes.headline: Better ask than guess
outcomes.text: The physicist explains, with obvious delight.

decisions.headline: Solar cells, so why batteries?
decisions.text: The craft has solar cells now. To save weight, the budget office proposes leaving out the batteries. The power engineers are outraged; the budget office asks you to explain why.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: Solar cells need a battery to start up

outcomes.headline: Not the reason
outcomes.text: The budget office replaces the batteries with a small starter cell. The power engineers spend a season putting the real ones back.

options.label: For the night side: every lap passes through Earth's shadow

outcomes.headline: Right
outcomes.text: In low orbit the craft spends up to about 40 % of every lap in shadow. The batteries stay, and get charged and drained thousands of times, so better ones are ordered.

options.label: In case the Sun goes quiet

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: The Sun doesn't go dark. The budget office decides the batteries are a luxury and cuts them in half.

outcomes.headline: The engineers explain
outcomes.text: The power engineers explain, at length.

decisions.headline: Why steer at all?
decisions.text: To save weight and cost, a manager suggests a simpler steering system that only works for the turn towards orbit. “It's going straight up anyway for the first part,” the manager says. “Why steer that?”
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: Fair point: straight up, it flies itself

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: The study of the simpler system runs for a season before a guidance engineer kills it.

options.label: Fins keep it straight; steering is for higher up

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: Fins help only in thick air, and many rockets have none. The study wastes a season.

options.label: Pushed from the bottom, it tips over unless it's steered every moment

outcomes.headline: Right: a broom on a hand
outcomes.text: Like a broom balanced on a palm, any small tip grows. The steering stays, and the manager asks good questions about the gyroscopes instead.

outcomes.headline: Better ask than guess
outcomes.text: A guidance engineer explains with a broom from the cleaners' cupboard.

decisions.headline: Why spin the top stages?
decisions.text: The small upper stages have no steering of their own. The design has them spun up by a motor before launch, and an accountant wants to know why the motor is in the budget.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: A spinning stage keeps pointing the way it was aimed

outcomes.headline: Right: spin holds direction
outcomes.text: Like a top or a rifle bullet. The stage below aims them, and the spin keeps them on that line with nothing to go wrong. The motor stays.

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: Solid propellant doesn't need mixing. The accountant now thinks the motor is a frill, and it takes a season to win it back.

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: The nozzles are no cooler for spinning. The budget meeting turns into a long argument.

outcomes.headline: Better ask than guess
outcomes.text: A guidance engineer spins a coin on the table to explain.

decisions.headline: What makes it safe enough?
decisions.text: A committee visiting the works asks what the most important change is when a rocket built as a missile is made fit to carry a person.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: A thicker skin, to survive more

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: Thicker skin means less payload, and doesn't help when an engine falters. The committee asks for a study of thicker skins anyway.

options.label: A system that senses trouble and gets the crew out

outcomes.headline: Right
outcomes.text: It watches the rocket and acts faster than a person could. The committee leaves impressed and recommends more money for testing.

options.label: Bigger engines, for a margin of thrust

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: More thrust is not more safety. The committee's report asks for an engine study the team doesn't need.

outcomes.headline: The chief designer answers
outcomes.text: The chief designer takes the question and the committee moves on.

decisions.headline: Catching up in orbit
decisions.text: A test pilot joining the agency is shown a craft that has to catch another one a few kilometres ahead of it in the same orbit. The pilot asks what you'd do.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

outcomes.headline: Wrong: it climbs and falls behind
outcomes.text: The extra speed lifts the craft into a higher, slower orbit, and the target pulls away. The pilot's instinct and yours agree, and both are wrong.

options.label: Brake, drop lower, and gain on it

outcomes.headline: Right: brake to catch up
outcomes.text: A lower orbit is a quicker lap. Gain on the target from below, then burn forward to rise and meet it. The pilot whistles.

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: Gemini 4's crew tried exactly that in 1965 and watched their target slip away. A season goes on unlearning it.

outcomes.headline: Better ask than guess
outcomes.text: An orbit specialist sketches the two orbits on a napkin.

decisions.headline: Four minutes of silence
decisions.text: In every return through the air, the craft's radio goes silent for a few minutes, then comes back. The radio team wants a stronger transmitter. You're asked whether it would help.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: Yes: the signal is just too weak at that distance

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: A heavier transmitter is built and goes silent in exactly the same place.

options.label: No: the hot air around the craft carries electricity and blocks radio

outcomes.headline: Right
outcomes.text: The glowing air around the craft swallows the signal until it cools. The radio team stops worrying, and the weight goes to the heat shield instead.

options.label: No: the antenna burns off and a spare comes out

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: There is no spare antenna. The team spends a season designing one.

outcomes.headline: Better ask than guess
outcomes.text: The heat shield team explains and the radio team stands down.

decisions.headline: Only a little higher
decisions.text: An official reviewing the budget points out that an orbit is barely higher than a flight that goes up and comes straight down. Why, then, does orbit need a rocket several times the size?
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: It's not height but speed: about eight kilometres a second, sideways

outcomes.headline: Right
outcomes.text: Several times the speed and many times the energy, all from the rocket. The official signs the budget with a new respect.

options.label: The rocket has to push through much more air

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: Both flights cross the same air. The official orders a study of streamlining, which costs the team a season.

options.label: Orbit is really ten times higher

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: It isn't. The official catches the mistake and trusts the team's figures less for a while.

outcomes.headline: Better ask than guess
outcomes.text: The chief designer explains with Newton's cannon.

decisions.headline: Why not one big stage?
decisions.text: A designer from an aircraft firm, new to rockets, proposes a single big stage instead of several: fewer separations, fewer things to go wrong. The room goes quiet and waits for you.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: The one-stage study shows the rocket would carry nothing but itself. It takes a season to find that out.

options.label: Dropping empty tanks and engines saves lifting dead weight

outcomes.headline: Right: throw weight away
outcomes.text: An orbital rocket is mostly propellant. Throwing away the empty parts on the way up is the only way the payload fits in the last few per cent.

options.label: Small engines are safer than big ones

outcomes.headline: Not the reason
outcomes.text: Big engines can be safe too. The designer goes away unconvinced, and the argument comes back every week.

outcomes.headline: Better ask than guess
outcomes.text: An old rocket hand explains, with the rocket equation.

decisions.headline: Two pumps, side by side
decisions.text: A design has two pumps side by side, where either one alone can do the job. Each is 90 % reliable. The reviewer asks how reliable the pair is.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: That would be true if both had to work. The team removes the second pump to save weight, and puts it back a season later.

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: The backup counts for something. The team decides the second pump isn't worth its weight and argues about it for weeks.

outcomes.headline: Right: both must fail
outcomes.text: The pair fails only when both fail: one chance in ten times one in ten. The team puts backups on two more vital parts.

outcomes.headline: Better ask than guess
outcomes.text: The reviewer works it through on the blackboard.

decisions.headline: Why fuel it on the day?
decisions.text: An army officer on a tour asks why the rocket is fuelled only on launch day, when the army's missiles stand fuelled in their silos for months.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: Liquid oxygen boils away and has to be topped up to the last minutes

outcomes.headline: Right
outcomes.text: At minus 183 °C it never stops boiling. The missiles use propellants that stay liquid at room temperature, at the price of poison. The officer is satisfied, and so are the engineers.

options.label: The fuel goes stale in the tanks

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: The officer repeats it at headquarters, and the team spends a season answering a request for fresher fuel.

options.label: A fuelled rocket is too heavy to stand on its legs for long

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: It stands fine. The officer sends structural engineers to look, and they cost the team weeks.

outcomes.headline: Better ask than guess
outcomes.text: The propulsion lead answers for you.

decisions.headline: Why a small parachute first?
decisions.text: The recovery system opens a small parachute high up and the big one much lower. A cost review asks why one big parachute, opened early, wouldn't do the same job for less.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: The small one is a spare in case the big one fails

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: The review decides a spare is optional, and the small chute goes. It takes a season to put it back.

options.label: Opened at high speed, the big one would tear: the small one slows and steadies it first

outcomes.headline: Right
outcomes.text: The drogue takes the hard first jolt and steadies the fall, so the main can open gently lower down. The review signs off.

options.label: One for the craft, one for the heat shield

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: Nobody parachutes the heat shield down. The review asks why it needs one, and the meeting goes in circles for a week.

outcomes.headline: Better ask than guess
outcomes.text: The recovery engineers explain.

decisions.headline: Solar cells, out there?
decisions.text: At the Friday seminar a student asks whether a probe to Jupiter could run on solar cells like the satellites closer to home. The speaker turns the question over to you.
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: Yes: space is just as sunny everywhere

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: The seminar goes wrong from there, and so does a week of power studies after it.

options.label: Yes, with panels twice the size

outcomes.headline: Not nearly enough
outcomes.text: Twice as far gets a quarter of the light. A study of bigger panels runs for a season before anyone checks the arithmetic.

options.label: No: sunlight there is about 4 % of ours, so it needs a heat-powered generator

outcomes.headline: Right
outcomes.text: Light thins with the square of the distance. The outer probes ran on the heat of decaying plutonium. The student goes away thinking, and so do the power engineers.

outcomes.headline: Better ask than guess
outcomes.text: The speaker answers and the seminar moves on.

decisions.headline: Why wait for Mars?
decisions.text: A minister asks why a probe to Mars can only go every two years or so. Couldn't a bigger rocket go whenever it likes?
decisions.stakes: The answers show nothing in advance. A right answer is worth about three seasons' gain, a wrong one costs about a season's.

options.label: That's when the dust storms on Mars die down

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: The minister asks for a study of Martian weather. It goes nowhere and takes a season.

options.label: The planets line up for the cheap path only every 26 months or so

outcomes.headline: Right: a launch window
outcomes.text: Outside the window the trip needs far more fuel than any rocket gives. The minister writes the next window's dates in a diary.

options.label: Yes: a big enough rocket could go any time

outcomes.headline: Wrong
outcomes.text: No rocket of the age could. The minister hears 'bigger rocket' and wants a costing for one.

outcomes.headline: Better ask than guess
outcomes.text: The flight planners prepare a short note for the minister.

decisions.headline: The night shift wants a say
decisions.text: The technicians on the night shift say nobody asks them anything, though they build most of the hardware. They want a meeting with the design team. The foreman says they should mind their benches.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

outcomes.headline: They had good ideas
outcomes.text: The technicians bring a list of small fixes that make the hardware easier to build right. The design team takes most of them.

outcomes.headline: A night of grievances
outcomes.text: The meeting turns into a list of complaints about pay and canteen food. Nothing useful comes of it, and the foreman feels undermined.

outcomes.headline: Order kept
outcomes.text: The night shift goes back to work. It's quieter than before.

outcomes.headline: A sullen night shift
outcomes.text: The technicians do exactly what they are told and nothing more. Small mistakes creep in.

outcomes.headline: A bonus goes a long way
outcomes.text: The night shift takes the money and the hint. The hardware coming off the benches is tidier.

outcomes.headline: They wanted to be heard, not paid
outcomes.text: The technicians feel bought off. The design team hears about it for weeks.

decisions.headline: Who gets the credit?
decisions.text: A fix that solved a stubborn problem came out of a late-night argument between two engineers. The agency magazine wants a name for its cover story.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

outcomes.headline: The whole team on the cover
outcomes.text: The photo of the team hangs in every office. People talk about the next fix already.

outcomes.headline: Credit spread thin
outcomes.text: The one who really cracked it feels passed over. The mood on the team sours.

options.label: Keep it out of the magazine

outcomes.headline: No story
outcomes.text: The fix goes into the drawings and nobody's name goes into print.

outcomes.headline: A star is made
outcomes.text: The lead engineer is fired up by the attention and drives the team hard.

outcomes.headline: Resentment
outcomes.text: The others know who really did it. The team stops talking at lunch.

decisions.headline: A writer wants a month with the team
decisions.text: A well-known magazine writer asks to spend a month in the workshop, watching the team at work, for a long story about the people behind the hardware. The security office says it's up to you.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

outcomes.headline: A story people read
outcomes.text: The story is warm and true, and the government likes how the agency looks in it. A little extra money follows.

outcomes.headline: Quoted at a bad moment
outcomes.text: The story leads with an engineer swearing at a broken part. The team feels made fun of in print.

options.label: Let the writer in with a press officer alongside

outcomes.headline: A careful, dull story
outcomes.text: With a press officer at every elbow, nobody says anything interesting. The story is polite and soon forgotten.

outcomes.headline: Watched at work
outcomes.text: Two people with notebooks in the workshop all month. The team works stiffly, and small mistakes creep in.

outcomes.headline: No story
outcomes.text: The writer goes to an aircraft factory instead.

decisions.headline: The lucky jar
decisions.text: Since one good test, the team passes round a jar of sweets before every important run, and nobody may start until it has gone round. The quality office says it's unprofessional and wants it stopped.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

outcomes.headline: The jar goes round
outcomes.text: The team laughs at itself a little, and works better for it. Two good runs in a row, and the jar is now sacred.

outcomes.headline: Luck instead of checks
outcomes.text: A run goes badly after someone skipped the jar, and for a week the team argues about the jar instead of the fault.

outcomes.headline: The jar disappears
outcomes.text: The jar goes, and with it some of the fun. The team grumbles, but works.

outcomes.headline: Back to the checklist
outcomes.text: Without the jar, the pre-run checklist gets the attention instead. Nobody misses it for long.

outcomes.headline: The jar stays, unofficially
outcomes.text: The quality office mutters and moves on.

decisions.headline: A sketch on a napkin
decisions.text: A junior engineer brings you a napkin with an unusual fix for a problem the seniors have been stuck on for weeks. The seniors say it can't work. The junior is sure it can.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

options.label: Give the junior a week to try it

outcomes.headline: The napkin was right
outcomes.text: The odd fix works on the bench, first time. The seniors study it, then adopt it.

outcomes.headline: It couldn't work
outcomes.text: It doesn't. The seniors are smug about it, and the week is gone.

options.label: Have the seniors review it properly

outcomes.headline: Two ideas made one
outcomes.text: The seniors find what's right in the sketch and fix what's wrong. The result is better than either.

outcomes.headline: Politely dismissed
outcomes.text: The review is short and polite. The napkin goes in a drawer.

outcomes.headline: Back to the problem
outcomes.text: The seniors go on with their own approach.

outcomes.headline: A junior stops speaking up
outcomes.text: The junior engineer stops bringing ideas to anyone. The team is a little quieter, and a little worse.

decisions.headline: The safety officer stops the crane
decisions.text: The safety officer has found a frayed cable on the overhead crane and wants all lifting stopped until a new one comes, which may take a week. The workshop says it can lift carefully in the meantime.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

outcomes.headline: A week of paperwork
outcomes.text: With the crane down, the team catches up on drawings and checks. The new cable arrives, and nobody was hurt.

outcomes.headline: A lost week
outcomes.text: The cable takes three weeks, not one. The work stalls and the team gets restless.

outcomes.headline: Slow lifts, no trouble
outcomes.text: Light loads, two people watching every lift, and the new cable fitted without incident.

outcomes.headline: A load came down
outcomes.text: The cable parted with a light load on it. Nobody was under it, but the part it held was wrecked, and the team is shaken.

options.label: Leave it to the workshop foreman

outcomes.headline: The foreman decides
outcomes.text: The foreman splits the difference: small lifts only, and loud complaints to the supplier.

decisions.headline: A milestone to celebrate
decisions.text: The team has just passed a milestone that took months. The engineers hint that a celebration would be welcome. The schedule says there's no time.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

outcomes.headline: A night to remember
outcomes.text: Speeches, music and a cake shaped like the hardware. The team comes back the next week with new energy.

outcomes.headline: The morning after
outcomes.text: The party ran late. The next morning a tired technician fitted a part upside down, and it wasn't caught for days.

outcomes.headline: A long weekend
outcomes.text: A quiet day at home, and the team comes back rested.

outcomes.headline: Half of them came in anyway
outcomes.text: The building was half full on the day off. Nothing changed, except the coffee ran out.

outcomes.headline: On to the next one
outcomes.text: The milestone is noted on the board and the work goes on.

outcomes.headline: Months of work, no thanks
outcomes.text: The team feels nobody noticed. The next milestone comes no faster for it.

decisions.headline: An anonymous note
decisions.text: A note under your door says some test records were signed without the tests ever being run. It isn't signed and names nobody. It could be true, or it could be a grudge.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

outcomes.headline: It was true
outcomes.text: Three records were signed on trust after a long week. The tests are run properly, and one of them fails. Better now.

outcomes.headline: A witch-hunt
outcomes.text: The inquiry finds nothing, and everyone suspects everyone else of writing the note. The team doesn't trust itself for weeks.

options.label: Quietly rerun the last month's tests

outcomes.headline: One test fails on the rerun
outcomes.text: A test that was signed off fails when it is actually run. It's fixed, and nobody has to be named.

outcomes.headline: Every test passes again
outcomes.text: Every test passes a second time. Either the note was wrong, or nothing came of it.

outcomes.headline: Into the bin
outcomes.text: The note goes into the wastepaper basket. No more come.

decisions.headline: Move to the new hall now?
decisions.text: A new assembly hall is finished early: bigger, brighter, with a better crane. The team could move in now, in the middle of the work, or wait until this phase is done.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

outcomes.headline: Room to work
outcomes.text: The move takes a weekend. In the new hall everything is in reach and the work speeds up.

outcomes.headline: Lost in the move
outcomes.text: Crates of parts were mislabelled, and a box of calibrated tools turned up a month later. The work goes backwards for a while.

outcomes.headline: The hall can wait
outcomes.text: Another team moves into the new hall first.

decisions.headline: A famous physicist wants to sit in
decisions.text: A celebrated physicist, retired and bored, asks to sit in on the team's design reviews for a few weeks. Brilliant, everyone agrees. Difficult, everyone agrees too.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

outcomes.headline: One question changed everything
outcomes.text: The visitor asks one simple question nobody had asked, and the answer changes a design the team was proud of. For the better.

outcomes.headline: Lectures, every meeting
outcomes.text: Every review turns into a lecture. The engineers stop presenting anything they aren't sure of, which is most things.

options.label: Invite them to one big review

outcomes.headline: A memorable afternoon
outcomes.text: One review, three sharp questions and a long dinner. The team talks about it for weeks.

outcomes.headline: The visitor nodded off
outcomes.text: The visitor slept through the propulsion section and left early.

outcomes.headline: A tour and a handshake
outcomes.text: The visitor sees the hall, shakes hands and goes home.

decisions.headline: The lead shouts
decisions.text: Three engineers come to you together: the team's lead shouts at people in front of everyone, and two of the youngest are talking about asking for a transfer. The lead's work is excellent.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

options.label: Have a quiet word with the lead

outcomes.headline: A calmer workshop
outcomes.text: The lead hadn't realised how it landed, and apologises to the team. The workshop is quieter, and people speak up again.

outcomes.headline: The lead took it badly
outcomes.text: The lead asks who complained, and the next weeks are colder than ever.

outcomes.headline: They toughen up
outcomes.text: The engineers go back to work. The shouting goes on, and so does the excellent work.

outcomes.headline: Nobody speaks up now
outcomes.text: The team learns to keep its head down. Problems are found later than they should be.

outcomes.headline: It blew over, for now
outcomes.text: A good week on the bench, and fewer raised voices. The complaint isn't repeated.

outcomes.headline: It got worse
outcomes.text: A shouting match on the workshop floor, in front of a visiting supplier. Everyone is ashamed.

decisions.headline: A date in the newspapers
decisions.text: Someone at headquarters told the press when this hardware will be ready. It's an optimistic date, and the team read it in the morning paper like everyone else.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

options.label: Hold the team to the date

outcomes.headline: They rose to it
outcomes.text: The team takes it as a challenge. The work moves faster than anyone believed it could.

outcomes.headline: Corners cut
outcomes.text: To make the date, tests are shortened and checks skipped. The hardware is behind where it looks.

options.label: Have the press office correct it

outcomes.headline: A sigh of relief
outcomes.text: A small correction on page six, and the team relaxes. The work goes on at its own pace.

outcomes.headline: An embarrassing correction
outcomes.text: The newspapers make a meal of the correction, and the team reads every word of it.

outcomes.headline: Everybody forgets
outcomes.text: The date is never mentioned again, by anyone.

decisions.headline: The technicians want more for overtime
decisions.text: The technicians' representative asks for overtime to be paid at a better rate. They have worked a lot of it lately. Headquarters says the rate is the rate.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

outcomes.headline: Goodwill on the benches
outcomes.text: The technicians take the extra money as respect. The next push is easier to ask for.

outcomes.headline: And then the next request
outcomes.text: A week later the canteen staff and the drivers ask for the same. The goodwill is lost in the argument.

options.label: Offer time off in lieu instead

outcomes.headline: A fair trade
outcomes.text: Most of them would rather have the days off anyway. Rested technicians make fewer mistakes.

outcomes.headline: Short-handed
outcomes.text: Everyone takes their days at once. The workshop runs half empty for a fortnight.

outcomes.headline: They accept it
outcomes.text: The technicians grumble and go back to their benches.

outcomes.headline: Not a minute more
outcomes.text: No more overtime from anyone. The work slows to the pace of the written hours.

decisions.headline: A suggestion box?
decisions.text: The personnel office wants to put a suggestion box in the workshop, anonymous, opened once a month. The engineers are divided: some think it's a good idea, some think it's an invitation to gripe.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

outcomes.headline: Small, good ideas
outcomes.text: The first month's box holds a dozen small, practical fixes from people who never speak in meetings.

outcomes.headline: Mostly insults
outcomes.text: The box fills with rude notes about named people. It comes down after a month, and the bad feeling stays.

options.label: Put up the box, with a prize for the best idea

outcomes.headline: A competition
outcomes.text: With a prize on offer, people put real thought into it. The winning idea saves a whole assembly step.

outcomes.headline: A row over the prize
outcomes.text: Two people claim the winning idea was theirs first. The prize is shared, grudgingly.

outcomes.headline: No box
outcomes.text: Suggestions go to the team lead, as they always have.

decisions.headline: A challenge from the launch crew
decisions.text: The launch crew has challenged the engineers to a football match, loser buys the drinks. The engineers are not athletes. Some of them want to play anyway.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

outcomes.headline: A famous victory
outcomes.text: Against all odds, the engineers win, two goals to one. Nobody talks about anything else for a week.

outcomes.headline: Thrashed, happily
outcomes.text: Seven goals to nil, and a fine evening afterwards. The engineers and the launch crew get on better than ever.

outcomes.headline: A sore defeat
outcomes.text: Heavy defeat, sore ankles and a week of jokes from the launch crew. Some of the engineers take it badly.

outcomes.headline: No match
outcomes.text: The launch crew calls the engineers cowards, cheerfully.

decisions.headline: A delegation wants a tour
decisions.text: A delegation from a friendly country is visiting, and the foreign ministry would like them shown something impressive. The obvious thing to show is this team's hardware, in the middle of its work.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

outcomes.headline: A delegation impressed
outcomes.text: The visitors are wide-eyed, the ministry is pleased, and a thank-you comes with a little more money.

outcomes.headline: A diplomatic gaffe
outcomes.text: An engineer, asked a polite question, gives a rude answer. The ministry complains, and the team spends days tidying for nothing.

options.label: Show them the models in the lobby

outcomes.headline: Models and coffee
outcomes.text: The delegation admires the models and the coffee. The ministry would have liked more.

decisions.headline: A paper for the conference
decisions.text: One of the engineers has written a paper about the team's work for a big engineering conference. It's good work, and it says a lot. The security office would rather it said less.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

outcomes.headline: A standing room only talk
outcomes.text: The talk is a hit, and three experts in the audience offer useful advice afterwards. The team is proud.

outcomes.headline: Torn apart in questions
outcomes.text: A senior academic picks the paper apart in front of everyone. Some of the criticism is fair, and all of it stings.

options.label: Present it with the details cut

outcomes.headline: A thin talk
outcomes.text: With the details gone, there isn't much left. The talk passes without comment.

outcomes.headline: Gutted
outcomes.text: The author feels the paper was gutted, and tells everyone so.

outcomes.headline: Withdrawn
outcomes.text: The paper goes back in a drawer. Maybe after the flight.

decisions.headline: An old hand wants to help
decisions.text: A retired engineer who built the agency's first hardware has been seen in the canteen again. The offer is to help out for free, a few days a week. Some of the team are delighted; some are not.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

outcomes.headline: Old tricks, new hardware
outcomes.text: The old hand knows a dozen workshop tricks that were never written down, and teaches them gladly.

outcomes.headline: The old way, again and again
outcomes.text: Every change is met with 'that's not how we did it'. The younger engineers stop arguing and start avoiding the canteen.

options.label: Ask for one written report instead

outcomes.headline: A useful little report
outcomes.text: Ten handwritten pages, half of them very useful.

outcomes.headline: Hurt feelings
outcomes.text: The old hand writes a single page and stops coming to the canteen.

outcomes.headline: Thanks, but no
outcomes.text: The old hand takes it with good grace.

decisions.headline: Two designs, two camps
decisions.text: Two engineers have each designed a different answer to the same problem, and the team has split behind them. Each camp says the other's design will fail.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

outcomes.headline: The test settled it
outcomes.text: One design passes and the other fails, and nobody can argue with the test stand. The camps make peace.

outcomes.headline: A winner and a sore loser
outcomes.text: The better design wins, but its loser won't let it go. The team stays split.

outcomes.headline: Better together
outcomes.text: Locked in a room for a week, the two come out with a design that takes the best of both.

outcomes.headline: Designed by committee
outcomes.text: The joint design keeps the weaknesses of both. Nobody is happy with it.

outcomes.headline: The lead decides
outcomes.text: The lead picks one. Half the team is pleased.

decisions.headline: An engineer owns up
decisions.text: An engineer comes to you, pale: a calculation they signed off months ago was wrong, and the part is already built. Nobody else had noticed.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

options.label: Thank them in front of the team

outcomes.headline: Others come forward
outcomes.text: Within a week, two more people bring their own doubts forward. One of them is a real problem, found early.

outcomes.headline: Seen as a weakness
outcomes.text: Some on the team think it was rewarded for a mistake. The engineer is teased for weeks.

outcomes.headline: Fixed, and not mentioned
outcomes.text: The part is remade and the paperwork corrected. Nobody needs to know.

options.label: Put a note in their file

outcomes.headline: A lesson noted
outcomes.text: The engineer double-checks everything from now on.

outcomes.headline: Nobody owns up again
outcomes.text: Word gets round that owning up gets a note in your file. The next mistake is hidden, and found much later.

decisions.headline: Knock down the walls?
decisions.text: The building office offers to take out the walls between the team's small offices and make one big open room, so everyone can see and hear what everyone else is doing.
decisions.stakes: What each answer leads to can't be told in advance.

outcomes.headline: Everyone talking
outcomes.text: Questions get answered across the room in seconds. The work moves faster.

outcomes.headline: Nobody can think
outcomes.text: The room is loud all day. The people who need quiet start working at home in the evenings, tired.

outcomes.headline: Doors and walls
outcomes.text: Everyone keeps their own door.

decisions.headline: Who will oversee the test firing?
decisions.text: The test stand is booked for a firing of the stage, but its usual test conductor is ill. Somebody has to run the countdown, read the gauges and call the abort if it comes to that.
decisions.stakes: The better the engineer in this component's skill, the better the chance of a clean run.

outcomes.headline: {name} ran a clean test
outcomes.text: {name} called every step on time and caught a sticking valve before ignition. The firing told the team what it needed.

outcomes.headline: {name} aborted too late
outcomes.text: {name} hesitated over a warning light, and the engine ran rough for two seconds too long. Parts of the stand need replacing.

options.label: Nobody, the test is put off

outcomes.headline: The firing is put off
outcomes.text: The stand stays booked for later.

decisions.headline: Who signs off the vibration test?
decisions.text: The shake table is ready to rattle the hardware the way a launch would. Somebody experienced has to decide how hard to shake it and what counts as a pass.
decisions.stakes: The better the engineer in this component's skill, the better the chance the test finds the weak spots.

outcomes.headline: {name} found the weak spot
outcomes.text: {name} ran the table hard enough to shake a bracket loose on the ground instead of in flight.

outcomes.headline: {name} shook it to pieces
outcomes.text: {name} set the table too hard and broke a test unit that was fine.

options.label: Run the standard test
options.shows: Sure to give about half a season's gain.

outcomes.headline: A standard shake
outcomes.text: The book test passes without surprises.

decisions.headline: Who audits the supplier?
decisions.text: A small supplier makes a part nobody else can, and its last batch had two rejects. Someone needs to spend a week in its factory, checking how the part is really made.
decisions.stakes: The better the engineer in this component's skill, the better the chance the audit finds the cause.

outcomes.headline: {name} found the shortcut
outcomes.text: {name} spotted a step the night shift skips to save time. The supplier's manager was mortified, and the next batch is perfect.

outcomes.headline: {name} saw the show
outcomes.text: The factory put on a fine show for {name}, who came back reassured. The next batch has rejects too.

outcomes.headline: A stern letter
outcomes.text: The supplier promises to do better.

decisions.headline: Who keeps the clean room clean?
decisions.text: Final assembly moves into the clean room, where a hair or a fleck of dust can short a circuit or fog a lens. Someone has to set the rules and make everyone keep them, including the senior people.
decisions.stakes: The better the engineer in this component's skill, the better the chance nothing gets in.

outcomes.headline: {name} ran a spotless room
outcomes.text: {name} made even the chief designer put on the hood and the overshoes. The craft came out of assembly without a speck inside.

outcomes.headline: A stray washer
outcomes.text: Under {name}, a washer was left loose inside the craft. It turned up rattling in the shake test, and a panel had to come off.

outcomes.headline: By the book
outcomes.text: The rules are posted on the door and mostly followed.

decisions.headline: Who leads the failure review?
decisions.text: A test unit failed last week and the team's own explanation is a little too convenient. An engineer from outside the team should lead the review, ask the awkward questions and sign the conclusion.
decisions.stakes: The better the engineer in this component's skill, the better the chance the real cause is found.

outcomes.headline: {name} found the real cause
outcomes.text: {name} kept asking why until the convenient answer fell apart. The real cause was in a part nobody had suspected.

outcomes.headline: {name} signed the easy answer
outcomes.text: {name} accepted the team's explanation. The same failure came back a month later.

outcomes.headline: Reviewed in-house
outcomes.text: The team's explanation goes into the file.

decisions.headline: Who runs the tank pressure test?
decisions.text: The new tanks are ready for their pressure test, and how far to push them is a judgement call. Too gently and a weak seam slips through; too hard and a good tank is ruined.
decisions.stakes: The better the engineer in this component's skill, the better the judgement. High stakes: about two and a half seasons' gain, or a season and a half's lost.

options.label: An engineer, told to push them hard

outcomes.headline: {name} found the limit
outcomes.text: {name} took the tanks well past flight pressure and stopped just short of harm. Now everyone knows how much margin there is.

outcomes.headline: {name} split a good tank
outcomes.text: {name} pushed too far, and a sound tank split along its seam. A new one has to be built.

options.label: The usual test, by the book
options.shows: Sure to give about half a season's gain.

outcomes.headline: By the book
outcomes.text: The tanks pass the usual test, and a seam that wept a little is redone.

decisions.headline: Who runs the countdown rehearsal?
decisions.text: The launch crew wants a full dress rehearsal of the countdown, without propellant, to shake out the procedures. Someone who knows the rocket has to sit at the main console and call it.
decisions.stakes: The better the engineer in this component's skill, the more problems the rehearsal shakes out.

options.label: Put an engineer at the console

outcomes.headline: {name} called a sharp count
outcomes.text: {name} stopped the count eleven times, each for a real reason. The procedure is thirty pages shorter and much clearer.

outcomes.headline: {name} let it run
outcomes.text: {name} let small problems slide to keep the count moving. The rehearsal finished on time and taught nobody anything.

options.label: Let the launch crew run it alone
options.shows: Sure to give about half a season's gain.

outcomes.headline: The crew's own rehearsal
outcomes.text: The launch crew runs it by itself and finds a few problems of its own.

decisions.headline: Who checks the gauges?
decisions.text: The test lab's gauges haven't been calibrated against a standard in two years. If they're wrong, every test result is wrong with them. Someone careful needs to go through them all.
decisions.stakes: The better the engineer in this component's skill, the better the chance the bad gauges are found.

outcomes.headline: {name} found a liar
outcomes.text: {name} found one pressure gauge reading low by a tenth. Three old tests are rerun, and one of them fails.

outcomes.headline: {name} made it worse
outcomes.text: {name} calibrated against a standard that was itself out. Every gauge in the lab is now wrong the same way.

outcomes.headline: Next year
outcomes.text: The calibration goes on the list for next year.

decisions.headline: Who watches over the move?
decisions.text: A finished stage has to travel to the test site on a special trailer, through narrow roads and over two old bridges. Someone who knows where it can and can't take a knock should ride with it.
decisions.stakes: The better the engineer in this component's skill, the safer the journey.

outcomes.headline: {name} brought it through
outcomes.text: {name} stopped the convoy twice to re-tie straps nobody else had noticed slipping. The stage arrived without a scratch.

outcomes.headline: A dent at the bridge
